papers.title: Discrete Graph Structure Learning for Forecasting Multiple Time Series
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is an extensively studied subject in statistics, economics, and computer science. Exploration of the correlation and causation among the variables in a multivariate time series shows promise in enhancing the performance of a time series model. When using deep neural networks as forecasting models, we hypothesize that exploiting the pairwise information among multiple (multivariate) time series also improves their forecast. If an explicit graph structure is known, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been demonstrated as powerful tools to exploit the structure. In this work, we propose learning the structure simultaneously with the GNN if the graph is unknown. We cast the problem as learning a probabilistic graph model through optimizing the mean performance over the graph distribution. The distribution is parameterized by a neural network so that discrete graphs can be sampled differentiably through reparameterization. Empirical evaluations show that our method is simpler, more efficient, and better performing than a recently proposed bilevel learning approach for graph structure learning, as well as a broad array of forecasting models, either deep or non-deep learning based, and graph or non-graph based.

papers.title: Graph WaveNet for Deep Spatial-Temporal Graph Modeling
papers.abstract: Spatial-temporal graph modeling is an important task to analyze the spatial relations and temporal trends of components in a system. Existing approaches mostly capture the spatial dependency on a fixed graph structure, assuming that the underlying relation between entities is pre-determined. However, the explicit graph structure (relation) does not necessarily reflect the true dependency and genuine relation may be missing due to the incomplete connections in the data. Furthermore, existing methods are ineffective to capture the temporal trends as the RNNs or CNNs employed in these methods cannot capture long-range temporal sequences. To overcome these limitations, we propose in this paper a novel graph neural network architecture, Graph WaveNet, for spatial-temporal graph modeling. By developing a novel adaptive dependency matrix and learn it through node embedding, our model can precisely capture the hidden spatial dependency in the data. With a stacked dilated 1D convolution component whose receptive field grows exponentially as the number of layers increases, Graph WaveNet is able to handle very long sequences. These two components are integrated seamlessly in a unified framework and the whole framework is learned in an end-to-end manner. Experimental results on two public traffic network datasets, METR-LA and PEMS-BAY, demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithm.

papers.title: LargeST: A Benchmark Dataset for Large-Scale Traffic Forecasting
papers.abstract: Road traffic forecasting plays a critical role in smart city initiatives and has experienced significant advancements thanks to the power of deep learning in capturing non-linear patterns of traffic data. However, the promising results achieved on current public datasets may not be applicable to practical scenarios due to limitations within these datasets. First, the limited sizes of them may not reflect the real-world scale of traffic networks. Second, the temporal coverage of these datasets is typically short, posing hurdles in studying long-term patterns and acquiring sufficient samples for training deep models. Third, these datasets often lack adequate metadata for sensors, which compromises the reliability and interpretability of the data. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce the LargeST benchmark dataset. It encompasses a total number of 8,600 sensors in California with a 5-year time coverage and includes comprehensive metadata. Using LargeST, we perform in-depth data analysis to extract data insights, benchmark well-known baselines in terms of their performance and efficiency, and identify challenges as well as opportunities for future research. We release the datasets and baseline implementations at: https://github.com/liuxu77/LargeST.

papers.title: Graph Neural Controlled Differential Equations for Traffic Forecasting
papers.venue: AAAI Publications (The Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI))
papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting is one of the most popular spatio-temporal tasks in the field of machine learning. A prevalent approach in the field is to combine graph convolutional networks and recurrent neural networks for the spatio-temporal processing. There has been fierce competition and many novel methods have been proposed. In this paper, we present the method of spatio-temporal graph neural controlled differential equation (STG-NCDE). Neural controlled differential equations (NCDEs) are a breakthrough concept for processing sequential data. We extend the concept and design two NCDEs: one for the temporal processing and the other for the spatial processing. After that, we combine them into a single framework. We conduct experiments with 6 benchmark datasets and 20 baselines. STG-NCDE shows the best accuracy in all cases, outperforming all those 20 baselines by non-trivial margins.
papers.rationale: The paper presents STG‑NCDE and evaluates it against 20 baselines on six benchmark datasets, claiming superior accuracy. However, it does not discuss how forecast horizon or metric masking varies across experiments, nor does it analyze baseline robustness when those factors change. Thus it provides limited evidence for selecting defensible baselines under differing horizons or masking schemes.
papers.limitations: No explicit reporting of forecast horizon lengths, metric masking strategies, or ablation studies that would show baseline performance under varying horizons or masked metrics; the evaluation assumes identical experimental settings across all methods, limiting insight into baseline suitability when those conditions differ.

draft.abstract: We propose a controlled replication study of traffic-forecasting baselines, motivated by a source audit of GTS and Graph WaveNet. The GTS appendix corrects an earlier metric calculation, while Graph WaveNet explicitly excludes missing values during training and testing. These details show why reported values must retain their experimental context. The proposed study will align data splits, preprocessing, forecast horizons, and metric masking before evaluating models under one implementation. The present work audits published evidence and has not run forecasting experiments. All extracted numeric results remain provisional pending independent review.

relatedWork.text: The GTS paper reports original results and subsequently supplies corrected results in Appendix D. The authors explain that the earlier version calculated MAE, RMSE, and MAPE differently from the official DCRNN publication. Original and corrected tables must therefore remain distinct evidence records; a source quotation containing a number alone does not resolve this distinction.

Graph WaveNet reports results at 15, 30, and 60 minutes on METR-LA and PEMS-BAY. Its experimental section states that missing values are excluded from training and testing. This provides a stated evaluation detail that must be checked against the version and protocol of any candidate baseline.

comparisons.text: The original GTS METR-LA 60-minute MAE of 2.99 must be read with the Appendix D correction. The corrected table reports 3.41. These are source-reported values from different calculation versions, not new measurements produced by this audit. We exclude the original calculation from the proposed common-protocol baseline set.

The software identifies provisional context matches as well as conflicts. Neither a matched dataset label nor an unverified extraction establishes complete protocol equivalence. Each candidate pair still requires review of masking, preprocessing, table version, result provenance, and horizon aggregation before it is used to justify an experiment.

draft.study: Re-run GTS and Graph WaveNet on one explicitly versioned METR-LA dataset. Use one chronological train/validation/test split and one normalization implementation. Evaluate the same 15-, 30-, and 60-minute horizons separately, and distinguish these from averages over horizons. Define exactly which zero or missing targets are masked. Use the corrected metric implementation and record the code commit. Repeat training with shared seeds and report mean and standard deviation, with no selection of only the best run. Keep cited baseline values separate from independently reproduced results. These are proposed controls; no model-training experiment has been conducted.
